lesson.title: The Starting Gun: Why Chemists Prize the Initial Rate
lesson.summary: The initial rate is the instantaneous rate measured at the very start of a reaction, t = 0, and it is the single most useful rate measurement for figuring out how concentration controls reaction speed.
lesson.body:
Of all the instants at which you could measure an instantaneous rate, the one chemists rely on most is t = 0, the moment the reactants are first mixed. This is called the initial rate. It might seem like an arbitrary choice, but it solves a real experimental problem. As a reaction proceeds, reactant concentrations fall, product concentrations rise, and in many reactions the products can start reacting with each other or reverting back to reactants (a reverse reaction). Both effects complicate the relationship between concentration and rate. At t = 0, none of that has happened yet: the only species present are the reactants, at concentrations the chemist measured out and knows exactly, and there are no products around to complicate things. The initial rate is therefore the cleanest possible snapshot of how concentration alone affects rate.

Because the initial rate is just the instantaneous rate evaluated at t = 0, it is found the same way, as the slope of the tangent to the concentration versus time curve at the very start, or approximated using an average rate over a short interval beginning at t = 0. Using the same hypothetical reaction A leads to products from the previous two chapters, the exact instantaneous rate at t = 0 works out to 2.0 x 10^-3 M/s. You can approximate this experimentally with a short early interval: if [A] falls from 1.00 M at t = 0 s to 0.9801 M at t = 10 s, the average rate over that brief window is -(0.9801 M - 1.00 M)/(10 s - 0 s) = -(-0.0199 M)/10 s = 0.0199 M/10 s = 0.00199 M/s, or 1.99 x 10^-3 M/s.

That approximation, 1.99 x 10^-3 M/s, is remarkably close to the true initial rate of 2.0 x 10^-3 M/s, which is exactly the point: measuring the rate over a short enough interval right at the start gives you a trustworthy stand-in for the instantaneous rate at t = 0, without needing calculus in the lab. This is precisely the strategy real experiments use, mix the reactants, measure how much product forms or reactant disappears in the first few seconds, and treat that as the initial rate. Because the initial rate isolates the effect of starting concentrations before any complications set in, it becomes the essential building block for the next several chapters, starting with the rate law itself.
